name: The three ways plates meet (a plate-boundary field guide)
scope: The recognition base for the whole earthsystem strand: the three kinds of plate boundary, each anchored to its signature place. T1: at Iceland's Thingvellir you can stand in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates PULL APART -- a divergent boundary, the ground literally opening in fissures. T2: along South America's Pacific coast one plate DIVES beneath another and the Andes rise -- a convergent (subduction) boundary. T3: in California the Pacific and North American plates SLIDE PAST each other along the San Andreas Fault, neither made nor destroyed -- a transform boundary (invert the wonder: 'plates that only scrape sideways, making no new land' -> transform). T4: the crust is broken into a few giant slabs (the Pacific plate is the largest, flooring most of the ocean) that drift only a few centimetres a year -- about as fast as your fingernails grow. T5: in Ethiopia's Afar region THREE rift arms meet at one spot -- a triple junction where the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African rifts all pull in different directions.
source: Grokipedia (Plate tectonics; checked first, direct fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Plate tectonics; Thingvellir; Afar Triangle) + USGS 'This Dynamic Earth'.
framing_note: The vocabulary spine every other earthsystem ladder leans on -- keep it SCENE-LED and easy (open with Thingvellir's walkable crack, never 'define divergent'). Teach each term by its PLACE before testing it; the answer is the boundary TYPE recalled as knowledge, not deduced from a stem that already says 'pull apart' -- describe the place's drama, then ask the name. Distractors = the other real boundary types + 'a hotspot', all live. Dinner-test payoff: the fingernail-speed drift (T4) and the three-way Afar tear (T5). No same-fact overlap with the dedicated ladders -- this one hands out the map, they go deep.

name: The Ring of Fire: a rim of subduction volcanoes
scope: One process -- an ocean plate diving under a continent MELTS into a chain of volcanoes -- toured around the Pacific rim. T1: a horseshoe of volcanoes ~40,000 km long rings the Pacific and holds about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes (over 450 of them) -- the 'Ring of Fire'. T2: in the Andes the Nazca plate dives under South America and lifts Ojos del Salado on the Chile-Argentina border -- at 6,893 m the highest volcano on Earth, with the world's highest lake in its summit crater. T3: in the U.S. Pacific Northwest the Cascade arc rises behind the Cascadia subduction zone -- Mount St. Helens tore its own north face off in the 1980 blast. T4: on Indonesia's Sunda arc, Tambora's 1815 eruption was the largest in recorded history and chilled the whole planet into 1816's 'year without a summer'. T5: subduction volcanoes are the EXPLOSIVE kind -- seawater dragged down with the slab lowers the rock's melting point and makes sticky, gas-rich magma, unlike the runny lava of a hotspot shield like Hawaii (contrast a named Ring-of-Fire cone with a named hotspot volcano).
source: Grokipedia (Ring of Fire; Ojos del Salado -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Ring of Fire; Ojos del Salado; 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora; Mount St. Helens) + Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program.
framing_note: Theme = subduction builds a RING of volcanoes; every rung a different named cone/arc. Dinner-test payoff: Ojos del Salado the highest volcano with a lake in its crater (T2) and Tambora dimming the whole planet's sky (T4). Accuracy rail: '~75% of active volcanoes / 90% of quakes' is the standard USGS figure -- state it as '~three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes'. Lane border: an eruption's effect on CROPS/famine leans history -- keep answers on the volcano and its plate, never the human toll. Distractors = other real Ring-of-Fire volcanoes/arcs, all live.
history_overlap: Tambora/Krakatoa/St. Helens may also surface as history disasters -- keep the geography answer the earth-process/place fact (the arc, the plate, the eruption's scale on the land), not a casualty narrative.

name: Megathrust: the deepest trenches and the strongest quakes
scope: The other face of subduction -- where the diving slab locks then lurches, it carves the deepest trenches and unleashes the biggest earthquakes and tsunamis on Earth. T1: where the old, cold Pacific plate bends down into the Mariana Trench it makes the deepest point in any ocean -- the Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m down; drop Mount Everest in and its summit would still be ~2 km underwater. T2: the largest earthquake ever recorded struck off Chile in 1960 -- magnitude ~9.5 on the Nazca-South America subduction zone, its tsunami crossing the entire Pacific to strike Japan. T3: Alaska's 1964 'Good Friday' quake (~M9.2) rode the Aleutian megathrust -- the second-largest ever measured. T4: Japan's 2011 Tohoku quake (~M9.0) shoved the main island of Honshu about 2.4 m eastward and nudged Earth's axis. T5: the Cascadia zone off Washington and Oregon last ruptured on the night of 26 January 1700 -- a date pinned down by an 'orphan tsunami' that flooded Japan's coast with no local earthquake to explain it -- and is now considered overdue.
source: Grokipedia (Challenger Deep; Cascadia subduction zone -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Challenger Deep; 1960 Valdivia earthquake; 1964 Alaska earthquake; 2011 Tohoku earthquake; Cascadia subduction zone; 1700 Cascadia earthquake) + USGS.
framing_note: Theme = the megathrust's superlatives (deepest trench, biggest quakes) toured by named place. Dinner-test payoff: the Challenger Deep swallowing Everest (T1) and the 1700 orphan-tsunami detective story (T5). Accuracy rail: the Pacific plate subducts beneath the small Mariana plate; the 1700 date really was fixed from Japanese tsunami records + Washington's drowned 'ghost forests'. Numbers here are EARNED payoffs (the stem builds the expectation the depth/magnitude then shatters), never cold trivia. Distractors = other real trenches / megathrust quakes, all live.
history_overlap: The 1960 Chile / 1964 Alaska / 2011 Tohoku / 2004 Sumatra quakes may appear as history episodes -- geography's answer must be the EARTH fact (the trench, the fault type, the plate, the orphan-tsunami dating trick), never the relief-effort or death-toll story.

name: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge: where the seafloor is born (and Iceland stands on it)
scope: One process -- two plates pulling apart and erupting fresh ocean floor into the gap -- shown where that ridge actually breaks the surface. T1: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is part of the longest mountain range on Earth: a ~65,000 km volcanic seam that runs along the seafloor around the whole globe, almost all of it hidden underwater. T2: Iceland is the rare place the ridge rises into daylight; at Thingvellir the rift opens as walkable cliffs and fissures between the North American and Eurasian plates. T3: at Iceland's Silfra fissure divers glide through crystal-clear glacial meltwater in the gap between two continental plates. T4: in November 1963 a brand-new island, Surtsey, erupted straight out of the sea off Iceland's south coast, and has been a sealed natural laboratory watched ever since. T5: Iceland only exists because it sits on the spreading ridge AND over a deep mantle hotspot at the same time -- double the magma, which is why the ridge here piles into a plateau above the waves instead of lying 2.5 km down.
source: Grokipedia (Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Thingvellir; Surtsey; Iceland hotspot -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Thingvellir; Silfra; Surtsey; Iceland plume) + USGS.
framing_note: Theme = spreading centres manufacture new crust; Iceland is the window onto it. Dinner-test payoff: Surtsey the island born in living memory (T4) and Silfra's swim between continents (T3). Accuracy rail: the Iceland plate boundary is a broad rift ZONE of many fissures, not one tidy crack -- Thingvellir/Silfra dramatize it, so frame 'walk/dive between the plates' as the beloved-but-simplified truth it is; the 'longest mountain range' means the whole mid-ocean-ridge system. Distractors = other real ridges/rift features + 'a hotspot island', all live.

name: Continents in collision: the great mountain belts
scope: One process -- two landmasses ramming together with nowhere left to subduct, so the crust crumples upward -- across the world's collision ranges. T1: India is still ploughing north into Asia, and the Himalayas are STILL rising -- up to ~10 mm a year at Nanga Parbat, the fastest uplift on Earth. T2: the very summit rock of Mount Everest (8,849 m) is marine limestone -- seafloor stone hoisted 8.8 km into the sky, so the highest point on Earth was once an ocean bottom. T3: the whole Tibetan Plateau -- an area the size of Western Europe raised ~4.5 km high -- was thickened and lifted by the same India-Asia collision that began ~50 million years ago. T4: the Alps rose as Africa pushed into Europe, and the summit of the Matterhorn is a fragment of the AFRICAN plate stranded on top of European rock. T5: the Appalachians of eastern North America were once as tall as the Himalayas -- raised when Pangaea assembled ~300 million years ago -- and have been worn down to green stubs ever since; their torn-off other half now stands in Scotland and Scandinavia.
source: Grokipedia (Geology of the Himalaya; Matterhorn; Appalachian Mountains -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Geology of the Himalaya; Mount Everest geology; Tibetan Plateau; Alps; Matterhorn; Appalachian Mountains) + USGS.
framing_note: Theme = continent-continent collision toured by named range; the Himalayas are the flagship. Dinner-test payoff: seafloor stone at the top of Everest (T2) and the African summit of the Matterhorn (T4). Accuracy rail: Everest's summit is Ordovician marine LIMESTONE bearing marine fossils (crinoid/shell fragments) -- keep the rung on 'marine limestone at the summit'; the famous Himalayan ammonite 'shaligrams' come from LOWER rock (the Kali Gandaki), so do not pin ammonites AT the summit. Lane border: the Ganges/Indus born of the range are geography, but keep answers on the mountains and their rock, not river culture. Distractors = other real ranges/collisions, all live.

name: The East African Rift: a continent tearing itself apart
scope: One process -- a continent splitting along a divergent boundary ON LAND -- toured down the East African Rift. T1: a vast crack ~6,000 km long runs from the Red Sea down through Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania, slowly prising Africa into two plates. T2: in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nyiragongo cradles one of the world's largest lava lakes; its lava is so runny and fast it raced downhill into the city of Goma in 2002. T3: Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai is the only volcano on Earth that erupts carbonatite lava -- unearthly cool (~510 C) black lava that turns snow-white within days as it weathers. T4: the rift floor cracked and dropped so deep it cradles Lake Tanganyika -- the world's second-deepest and among its oldest lakes, a sliver of water ~1.4 km deep. T5: geologists expect the Somali side to eventually split off entirely, and in roughly 10 million years the ocean to flood in and turn the Horn of Africa into a separate landmass.
source: Grokipedia (East African Rift; Ol Doinyo Lengai; Mount Nyiragongo -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (East African Rift; Ol Doinyo Lengai; Mount Nyiragongo; Lake Tanganyika) + Smithsonian GVP.
framing_note: Theme = a divergent boundary caught in the act on dry land. Dinner-test payoff: Ol Doinyo Lengai's cool black-then-white lava (T3) and Africa's coming ocean (T5). Lane border: rift-lake CICHLID fish swarms are the ANIMAL bank -- keep the answer the LAKE and its rift-made depth, never the fish's biology; the rift's early-human 'Cradle of Mankind' fossils lean HISTORY/anthropology, so keep answers on the landform/process. Accuracy rail: 'only active carbonatite volcano' and its ~510 C lava are established; frame the future ocean as the ~10-Myr geological prediction it is. Distractors = other real rift volcanoes/lakes, all live.

name: From rift to ocean: the Red Sea and the Afar Triangle
scope: The next chapter of rifting -- where the land-tear has already let the sea in and a real ocean is being born. T2: the Red Sea is a baby ocean -- Arabia is splitting away from Africa along a spreading ridge, and the sea is genuinely widening (a single 2005 rifting spasm in Afar opened the crust by several metres in weeks). T3: at the Afar Triangle in Ethiopia three rifts meet at a triple junction, one of the only places on Earth where mid-ocean-ridge spreading happens on dry land you can walk across. T4: Afar's Danakil Depression lies over 100 m BELOW sea level and holds Erta Ale, a volcano with a near-permanent boiling lava lake. T5: nearby Dallol paints the desert with acid-yellow, green and white hydrothermal terraces over a buried salt dome -- one of the hottest, most alien-looking landscapes anywhere on Earth.
source: Grokipedia (Red Sea; Afar Triangle; Erta Ale; Dallol -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Red Sea; Afar Triangle; 2005 Dabbahu rifting episode; Erta Ale; Dallol).
framing_note: Direct sequel to the East African Rift ladder, so open at T2 (no baby-tier); theme = a rift that has already become a sea. Dinner-test payoff: Erta Ale's permanent lava lake below sea level (T4) and Dallol's alien colours (T5). Accuracy rail: the 2005 Dabbahu episode really opened an ~8 m-wide, ~60 km-long crack in weeks; keep 'a new ocean' as the Wilson-cycle projection it is. Keep answers on the LANDFORM/process, not the region's modern politics. Distractors = other real rift/spreading features, all live.

name: Transform faults: the plates that grind past each other
scope: One process -- plates sliding sideways, making no new crust and destroying none, just loading stress until it snaps -- across the world's great strike-slip faults. T1: California's San Andreas Fault is where the Pacific plate scrapes northwest past North America; it does not collide, it SLIDES. T2: on the Carrizo Plain the fault is so bare you can see streambeds bent sideways where the ground has crept past -- and in 1906 it lurched up to ~6 m at once, wrecking San Francisco. T3: because the land west of the fault is drifting northwest, Los Angeles is slowly sliding toward San Francisco -- they will be neighbours in ~20 million years. T4: Turkey's North Anatolian Fault behaves like a zipper: since 1939 its big quakes have marched steadily westward toward Istanbul, each rupture loading the next segment. T5: the Dead Sea sits in a pull-apart gap along the Dead Sea Transform -- which is why the lowest dry land on Earth (~430 m below sea level) lies right on a sliding plate boundary.
source: Grokipedia (San Andreas Fault; North Anatolian Fault; Dead Sea Transform -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (San Andreas Fault; 1906 San Francisco earthquake; North Anatolian Fault; Dead Sea Transform) + USGS.
framing_note: Theme = transform boundaries, San Andreas the flagship. Dinner-test payoff: LA drifting toward SF (T3) and the offset streambeds you can walk on the Carrizo Plain (T2). Accuracy rail: San Andreas ~1,200 km, right-lateral, ~33-37 mm/yr; frame the LA-SF meet-up as the far-future projection it is. Teach 'transform / strike-slip' via the sliding scene before naming it. Not a current-events border topic -- keep it timeless earth science. Distractors = other real transform faults + subduction/rift red-herrings that stay live.
history_overlap: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake may also be a history episode -- keep the geography answer the FAULT/plate fact (transform boundary, the offset ground, the Carrizo Plain), never the fire-and-relief narrative.

name: Hotspots: the island chains a drifting plate builds
scope: One process -- a fixed plume of deep heat while the plate slides overhead, printing a line of volcanoes like a conveyor belt -- across the world's hotspot trails. T1: on Hawaii's Big Island, Kilauea still erupts, while the older islands to the northwest (Kauai is ~5 million years old) are long extinct and eroding -- the chain gets steadily older the farther you go from the hot spot. T2: read backwards, the Hawaiian-Emperor chain is a ~6,000 km trail of dead volcanoes recording exactly where the Pacific plate has drifted -- complete with a sharp ~47-million-year-old BEND where the plate changed course. T3: the next Hawaiian island, Kamaehuakanaloa (formerly Loihi), is already erupting -- but still a seamount hidden underwater off the Big Island's coast. T4: the same kind of plume sits under a CONTINENT at Yellowstone; as North America crept southwest, the hotspot left a trail of dead calderas across Idaho's Snake River Plain before parking under Wyoming. T5: India once drifted over the Reunion hotspot ~66 million years ago and it flooded the land with the Deccan Traps -- a lava field the size of a country -- while that same plume today still builds the island of Reunion far to the south.
source: Grokipedia (Hotspot (geology); Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain; Yellowstone hotspot; Reunion hotspot -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain; Yellowstone hotspot; Reunion hotspot; Deccan Traps) + USGS/Hawaiian Volcano Observatory.
framing_note: Theme = a stationary plume + a moving plate = an age-ordered island chain, the classic 'proof' of plate motion. Dinner-test payoff: the Hawaiian chain as a recording of the plate's whole path with its 47-Myr bend (T2) and the next island already growing underwater (T3). Lane border: Hawaii's/Galapagos's unique ANIMALS are the animal bank -- keep answers on the ISLANDS and their ages/geology, never the wildlife. Yellowstone here = the hotspot TRACK across the Snake River Plain (one rung); its geysers/caldera live in the dedicated Yellowstone ladder -- no same-fact overlap. Accuracy rail: the ~47-50 Myr bend's cause is debated (plate-motion change and/or plume drift) -- flag it as debated. Distractors = other real hotspot chains, all live.

name: Yellowstone: standing on the roof of a supervolcano
scope: The surface wonders of a continental hotspot, framed as the magma below written onto the ground. T1: Yellowstone holds more than 500 geysers -- more than the rest of the planet combined, roughly half of all Earth's geysers -- because a shallow magma chamber superheats the groundwater. T2: Old Faithful earns its name by firing a scalding column on a fairly predictable schedule, about every 60-90 minutes, as pressure rebuilds underground. T3: Grand Prismatic Spring rings sterile deep-blue water with bands of orange and green -- a bullseye where heat-loving microbes thrive in the cooler water toward the rim. T4: the reason you cannot 'see' the volcano is that you are standing INSIDE it -- the caldera left by Yellowstone's last supereruption ~640,000 years ago is roughly 60 km across, far too big to perceive from the ground.
source: Grokipedia (Yellowstone Caldera; Old Faithful; Grand Prismatic Spring -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Yellowstone Caldera; Old Faithful; Grand Prismatic Spring) + U.S. National Park Service.
framing_note: The tectonic/hotspot angle on Yellowstone (the magma below written on the surface) -- a companion to the hotspot ladder's TRACK rung, with no same-fact overlap. Dinner-test payoff: 'you are standing inside the crater' (T4) and half the world's geysers (T1). Lane border: a fuller scenic/wildlife Yellowstone likely lives in the NATURE section -- keep every rung here about the geothermal/volcanic system, not the bison or the canyon. Accuracy rail: '~half the world's geysers / >500' is the NPS figure; Grand Prismatic's colours come from thermophile microbes (context, not the animal bank). Distractors = other real geothermal features/calderas, all live.

name: Pangaea's ghost: how we know the map moves
scope: The evidence and the engine -- the deep 'why' behind the whole strand, still anchored to named places. T2: the Atlantic is still opening about as fast as your fingernails grow (~2.5 cm a year), so Europe and North America drift a little farther apart every single year. T3: the coastlines of West Africa and eastern South America fit together like puzzle pieces -- and matching fossils and rock belts run straight across the join -- the clue that convinced Alfred Wegener the continents once formed one land, Pangaea. T4: the Mediterranean is the shrinking leftover of an old ocean (the Tethys) being squeezed shut as Africa pushes into Europe -- and it once dried out almost completely into salt flats ~5.5 million years ago. T5: oceans open and close in a slow cycle -- new crust shoved out at spreading ridges, old crust dragged down by cold slabs sinking at trenches -- so today's scattered continents will gather into a new supercontinent hundreds of millions of years from now.
source: Grokipedia (Continental drift; Pangaea; Wilson cycle; Messinian salinity crisis -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Continental drift; Alfred Wegener; Pangaea; Messinian salinity crisis; Wilson cycle) + USGS 'This Dynamic Earth'.
framing_note: The capstone 'how do we KNOW' ladder -- keep it place-anchored (the African/South American coastline fit, the drying Mediterranean) so it never floats into abstraction. Dinner-test payoff: continents that fit like puzzle pieces (T3) and the Mediterranean once a dry salt basin (T4). Accuracy rail: attribute continental drift to Wegener (1912) and frame the matching FOSSILS as place-evidence (the same fossils appear on BOTH shores) without sliding into the organism's biology -- the wonder is the two continents once joined. Slightly harder ladder (few T1 rungs) -- the strand's easy openers live in the earlier ladders. Distractors = other real earth-history facts, all live.
